text:
Andy Burnham is being warned that 1.4 million workers will be at risk of being stuck in insecure jobs if a forthcoming ban on zero-hours contracts is watered down.
The prime minister is under pressure from business leaders to scale back last year’s Employment Rights Act, which is being introduced in stages over 2026 and 2027.
But the leader of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said it was “time for the government to deliver” on its manifesto promise.
“The business lobby has been pushing to ensure well over a million precarious workers miss out on security at work – that’s not right,” he said.
Business leaders are warning that Labour’s plan for the biggest shake-up of employment rights in a generation risks damaging jobs and growth at a perilous moment for the economy. Against the backdrop of the Middle East war, they say the measures add to employment costs and jeopardise Burnham’s pledges to kickstart growth and combat a youth jobs crisis.
Last week, employers seized on former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn’s landmark report into youth unemployment, which warned that the legislation risked hurting youth recruitment.
To the alarm of union leaders, charities and some Labour MPs, ministers are consulting on changes to zero-hours and similar contracts that would give employees the right to guaranteed hours.
The government is considering where to set an “hours threshold” to determine who would be eligible. A worker who is on a contract at or below that threshold would get a guaranteed hours offer.
Business leaders are pushing for a low threshold of eight hours a week, which would limit the number of workers the legislation would cover. Unions want either no barrier, or one that reflects full-time work of 48 hours a week. They argue that many employees routinely work over the hours specified in a contract.
Under an eight-hour threshold, a zero-hours worker who routinely worked 30 hours could have that arrangement guaranteed. But a worker with a contract for 12 hours a week but who regularly worked 30 hours would not.
The TUC warns this would simply lift the floor of insecurity from zero hours to eight.
Nowak said: “Let’s remember what this is all about – low-paid precarious workers who don’t know how much they’ll be earning from week to week or the hours they’ll be working. Workers whose hours can be withdrawn at the drop of a hat.
“Good employers have nothing to fear from these new rights. This will level the playing field for them – and stop the cowboys.”
The government has indicated a preference to set the threshold at between eight and 20 hours.
According to analysis by the TUC, about 1.4 million workers on variable-hours contracts would miss out if the threshold was set at eight hours a week. Official figures show there are 2.5 million workers on zero-hours contracts or who are agency workers paid at hourly rates on schedules that vary from week to week.
Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto. Under Keir Starmer, however, elements of the party’s plan to “make work pay” were watered down amid opposition from business.
Government analysis shows that estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.
Milburn called for ministers to apply a “cautionary principle” when overhauling zero-hours contracts to avoid adding to employers’ costs after a period of tax increases and high inflation sparked by the Iran war.
But unions are warning Burnham not to water down the plan, arguing that insecure, low-paid work is contributing to the youth jobs crisis.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, a shopworkers’ union, said: “Loopholes and watering down could leave millions of workers without the fair contract they were promised by the government in its manifesto.
“Even worse, some employers could game the system by only giving overtime to those who don’t qualify for the right, leaving the lowest-paid workers worse off than they are now.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are currently reviewing consultation responses to ensure we get the detail right.
“We are committed to tackling the one-sided flexibility that can result from zero hours and similar contracts, when workers bear all the financial risk of uncertain hours, shifts and earnings.”
digest_he: איגודי העובדים בבריטניה מנהלים מאבק נגד דרישות של מנהלי עסקים לרכך את החקיקה הממשלתית החדשה המיועדת לאסור חוזים ללא שעות עבודה קבועות. ראשי המשק מזהירים כי הרפורמה בתוך חוק זכויות העבודה עלולה לפגוע במשרות ובצמיחה הכלכלית על רקע עלויות מעסיקים גבוהות, ומבקשים לקבוע סף שעות נמוך של שמונה שעות בשבוע בלבד לזכאות לשעות מובטחות. מנגד, איגודי העובדים טוענים כי סף כזה יפקיר כ-1.4 מיליון עובדים במשרות ארעיות ולא בטוחות ויאפשר למעסיקים להתחמק מהתחייבויות. הממשלה שוקלת את תגובות הציבור להתייעצות ומדגישה את מחויבותה להתמודד עם הגמישות החד-צדדית שבה עובדים נושאים בכל הסיכון הכלכלי.
